turns.text: Another cat's mark. Laid down low across the base of the pole, under a day old, and it isn't mine. Ears go flat before the thought even finishes. Six lengths away, seven — whiskers do the counting so the rest of the body doesn't have to. Underneath the marking, something wrong: not gutter-water and fur, but a chemical bite, like a paw that's been standing in coolant instead of rain.

Server Alley 9 breathes around the claim — rows of rack towers stacked three high behind chain-link, each one humming its own note, the whole alley one long chord in B-flat. Coolant weeps down a pipe joint overhead, drip-drip-drip into a puddle that's gone rainbow with runoff oil. The scent trail bends left, toward a gap in the casing where the insulation's been gnawed back to bare copper — old work, teeth-sized, worried at over many nights. Two streets off, a maintenance drone's patrol chime ticks down from four minutes.

Low crouch, tail flat to the concrete, following the bend. The gap in the casing smells almost right — old enough that underneath the stranger's chemical bite there's a second layer, fainter, that the nose knows before the rest does. Teeth marks in the copper match teeth. This ground has been chewed before. By someone who wasn't a stranger at all.

The rack's hum shifts half a tone the second teeth close on fresh copper — a small electric flinch traveling up through the jaw. Somewhere past the casing a cracked little screen bolted to a support strut blinks awake, seized for three seconds: a fish, low-resolution, looping through the same six frames of water before the picture dissolves back to static. Warm. Steady. Two streets off, the patrol chime ticks past ninety seconds.

Freeze mid-bite. Not from the screen — from the air, which just went taut, the particular pressure-drop that means a rotor is deciding which way to look. Every hair along the spine stands up on its own schedule.

The drone crosses the alley mouth at rooftop height, searchlight dragging a cold white bar across wet concrete, across the chain-link, across the exact spot where fur used to be a second ago — but isn't now. From a speaker somewhere on its belly, tinned and cheerful: '...clean paws, clean profits, NekoCorp Suds — now with 12% more foam—' The light slides past. The chord of humming racks swallows the rest of the jingle whole.

/\/\_/\/\
    (  O   O  )
     \  ^Y^  /
      )=====(      -- ears up, rotor incoming --

Wait it out. Count the drip from the coolant pipe instead of breathing — four drops, five — until the pressure in the air lets go. Then back to the copper, back to the screen, the fish going in slow warm loops that don't need to mean anything to feel good to watch.

The signal steadies the longer teeth stay clamped to the wire — the fish-loop sharpens at the edges, one flickering frame less blurred than the last. Across the gap, on the lip of the opposite roofline, something catches the drone's afterglow and throws it back twice — two small mirrored discs where eyes should be, unmoving, aimed down into the alley. Not hunting-still. Watching-still. A different kind of quiet than the alley's own.

The growl that starts in the chest doesn't finish. Whatever's up there isn't crouched for a leap, isn't marking, isn't circling for the gap — just sitting at the edge with those flat bright disks turned this way, patient as the rain. Ears track it without turning the whole head. Not prey-shaped. Not threat-shaped either. Just shaped like something that sees more than it's saying.

The shape on the roofline unfolds without a sound — no scrape of claw on tar paper, no shift of weight the alley can feel — and by the time the coolant pipe drips twice more, the mirrored glint is gone, roofline empty, only a curl of steam rising off the gutter where nothing could have been standing at all.

Back to the wire. Bite reset, deeper this time, the copper bitter and metallic against the back teeth. The fish-loop holds clean for four whole seconds before folding back into static — longer than it held before. Ribs settle against the warm casing of the rack. This much, at least, is a held thing, not a stolen one anymore.

A different broadcast finds the alley now, threading in under the rack-hum from some fixed speaker two blocks over — not a jingle, no melody in it at all, just a flat voice looping through clause after clause, addendum fourteen, addendum fifteen, effective immediately, effective immediately, the words wearing a groove into the same six seconds over and over. It doesn't mean anything to the ear. It just itches, the way a door left open itches, the way a smell that shouldn't be there itches.

Ears flatten at the drone of it, not from danger but from the wrongness of the rhythm — no rise, no fall, no breath in it anywhere. Head turns away from the wire, weight shifting off the haunches, already deciding this spot's traded its quiet for something worse than a drone.

Overhead the coolant pipe hisses louder, pressure climbing somewhere upstream, and past the chain-link the sky flattens into the particular gray that means rain hasn't started yet but has already decided to. The patrol chime resets itself to four minutes. Somewhere in the stack of hums, one server drops a note and the whole chord leans slightly flat.

/\_/\        [ ENERGY: LOW ]
  ( >.< )       [ ]  [ ]  [ ]  [ ]
   > ~ <        one bar left, keep moving

One last pass at the pole before leaving it — nose down, throat working, laying a fresh line of scent right over the stranger's chemical-bitter mark, claiming the copper and the gap and the fish-loop all in the same motion. Then gone, low and quick, toward a narrower vent three casings down where the hum runs quieter.

The new gap swallows sound differently — tighter, closer, rain starting to tick against a grate somewhere above in single testing drops before committing to more. Warmth radiates off an older, slower machine here, its hum worn down to something almost gentle. No screens. No drone chime. Just heat, and the alley's chord fading to a background hush.

Curl in tight against the warm metal, one ear still up, still counting drips, still logging the alley's ordinary sounds against whatever might not be ordinary. The wire back at the pole is still open, still humming, still there for tomorrow. That's enough to close both eyes to.

Rain finds its rhythm on the grate above, steady now, and Server Alley 9 settles into its long nighttime chord — coolant drip, transformer hum, the distant tick of a patrol chime nobody down here is required to answer to. The city keeps humming its note whether anything is listening or not.
